What is the secret menu that can diagnose a slow computer?

What, exactly, do they tell you?

Both the Windows Performance tab and the Mac Activity Monitor capture tons of processes, but the five main ones that are helpful for diagnosing a slow computer are:

  • CPU usage: Your computer’s Central Processing Unit runs applications and software, performs calculations and generally acts as the “brain” of your computer. High CPU usage isn’t always bad, but if it’s high during certain operations, it could be a clue as to why your computer is dragging.
  • Memory (RAM): Random-access memory is your computer’s short-term memory. When you open an app, stream a movie or play a game, RAM is where your computer stores the data and files that the CPU needs right away while the application is in use.
  • Disk space: Your disk drive or hard drive is your computer’s long-term memory, where files, photos and other things that are not needed while applications are running are stored. But it can also store shorter-term files, especially if the RAM is inadequate.
  • Network processes: This information doesn’t pertain to your physical computer, per se, but a slow network connection can definitely be a reason it isn’t working as fast as it should on processes that require the internet.
  • GPU usage: This is your graphics processing unit, aka graphics card. It’s what’s needed to quickly render videos, movies, games and other graphics-heavy applications, as well as process your computer’s overall visuals.

How do you find these menus?

It’s easy, but there are few ways to get there, depending on your operating system.

Open the Performance tab on Windows computers

  • Use the Start button: Right-click on the Start button, select Task Manager and then navigate to the Performance tab on the left (it looks like a line graph).
  • Use the taskbar: Right-click on an empty part of the taskbar, select Task Manager and navigate to the Performance tab.
  • Use keyboard shortcuts: Hit Cntl + Shift + Esc at the same time to bring up the Task Manager directly. Alternatively, you can use Cntl + Alt + Del, and then select Task Manager from the menu.

Open the Activity Monitor on a Mac

  • Use Spotlight search: Hit the Command button and the space bar, then type in Activity Monitor and hit return. You can also find Spotlight by clicking the magnifying glass in the top right corner of your screen.
  • Use Finder: Open Finder on your dock, then go to the toolbar across the top and select Go > Utilities > Activity Monitor. If Finder is not in your dock, click any empty space on your desktop and the Finder toolbar will appear.
  • Use the Apps icon: Select the Apps icon from your dock, then type in Activity Monitor and hit return. Apps is a dedicated apps launcher within Spotlight that rolled out with the Tahoe update, but if you are running an older version you’ll know it as Launchpad.
  • Use a keyboard shortcut: Hit Fn + Shift + A to bring up the Apps search directly.

What are you looking for?

There’s a lot of information in the Performance tab and Activity Monitor, and some of the more technical fixes are beyond the scope of this article. But you can start with some basic troubleshooting. When your computer is running slowly, open the Task Manager or Activity Monitor and be ready to jot down what you see.

Here are some top line things to look for and correct or research further.

High CPU usage

Temporary spikes are not necessarily concerning, but if your CPU is consistently running near the maximum, the fan is loud or your computer is just plain slow, click over to the Processes tab on a PC (right above the Performance tab) or click the CPU column on a Mac. Close any resource-heavy apps that you’re not using, then restart and recheck.

Update or reinstall apps that continually use too many resources, and disable apps that start up automatically so they’re not constantly running in the background. You can also try cleaning your computer’s fan and vents with compressed air.

Low disk space and RAM

Heavy RAM usage often indicates too many things are running at once. Close apps you’re not using as well as browsers and/or excessive tabs that are open. Today’s browsers are much bigger resource hogs than they used to be, constantly loading and running videos, background scripts and ads. Restart. If the problem persists, consider adding more RAM.

If disk space is low, get rid of files, videos and images you no longer need. Close apps you’re not using, clear up space by running your computer’s disk cleanup function, and consider upgrading to a solid state drive instead of an older hard drive.

High GPU usage

If your Activity Monitor or Performance tab shows high graphics-card usage, close video games and graphics-heavy apps and browsers. Restart your computer. If you continue to see that the GPU usage is high, you may need to update your graphics card.

Network problems

If you’re having network connectivity problems, it’s always worth it to stop any downloads or heavy streaming activities that could be hung up. Restart your computer, make sure your router and/or modem are online, and run a speed test from your internet provider.

What else can you do to fix a slow computer?

It’s worth trying some general fixes. Here are more tips that can help speed up your PC or Mac.

  • Restart your computer. Yes, it sounds basic, but restarting does give your computer a little refresh by clearing out temporary files and closing background processes that might be hung up.
  • Close any programs you’re not using. Close extra tabs, browsers and apps. Change your startup settings so you don’t have a lot of programs running in the background that you’re not using.
  • Scan for malware. Viruses and malware can cause slowdowns, so run an antivirus program like Microsoft Defender Antivirus. For a Mac, Apple’s protection is built in and runs automatically.
  • Keep your computer updated. When your computer says you have software or operating-system updates available, download them. Recommended patches and anti-virus updates not only keep you safe from hackers—they can speed up a slow computer too.

articles.title: Need to Calm Down ASAP? Here’s How to Activate Your Vagus Nerve in 3 Minutes or Less and Keep Stress at Bay
articles.content:
I can usually tell when my anxiety has crossed from “I’m worried about this” into “I can’t seem to let this go” because the logic stops logic’ing. I might know, rationally, that whatever I’m spiraling about probably isn’t as catastrophic as it feels, but I still end up fixating on it until I’m dizzy and hyperaware of every thump in my chest.
That disconnect is frustrating … but it’s also potentially useful. The thing is, anxiety isn’t just spinning thoughts or sweaty palms; it’s happening in both your mind and your body at once. And that means you may be able to work on the physical side of the response instead of simply waiting for your brain to magically become reasonable.
The vagus nerve is one of the key players in that mind-body connection, helping your brain communicate with organs throughout your body and playing an important role in shifting you out of a stress response. If anxiety can send that whole system in one panicked direction, there’s a lot of interest in whether you can work from the body up to help steer it back toward calmer waters, and there’s some pretty convincing science behind it.
To learn how to stimulate the vagus nerve, I spoke with Richard Gevirtz, PhD, a psychology professor at the California School of Professional Psychology at Alliant University, and Christopher Austelle, MD, a board-certified psychiatrist and a clinical assistant professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at Stanford University. Read on to learn how to work with your nervous system to calm down a whole lot faster.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more wellness, science, humor, cleaning, travel, tech and fun facts all week long.
The vagus nerve is one of the body’s major communication routes. Though we colloquially refer to it in the singular, we actually have two vagal nerves. They travel from the brainstem through either side of the neck and then into the chest and abdomen, passing the heart, lungs and digestive tract along the way.
Comprised of more than 200,000 nerve fibers, the vagus nerve is also the primary nerve involved in the parasympathetic nervous system, explains Gevirtz. Quick biology refresh: Your sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous systems help manage many of the things your body does automatically. The sympathetic side helps mobilize you when something requires action, while the parasympathetic side helps bring things back toward rest and recovery afterward. Gevirtz describes the parasympathetic system as the “rest, digest and restore” side.
You need both: The goal isn’t to stay relaxed all the time—it’s to be able to ramp up when you need to, then settle again.
The vagus nerve can help calm some of the physical changes that happen when you’re anxious. As a major pathway of the parasympathetic nervous system, it helps regulate heart rate, breathing and digestion, as well as helps your body return toward rest after a stress response.
During stress, Gevirtz explains, sympathetic activity normally increases while parasympathetic activity temporarily drops, a process sometimes called vagal withdrawal. That shift helps your body gear up to respond; once the demand has passed, the balance should move back toward rest and recovery. You can see part of that process with every breath. Your heart rate naturally rises slightly as you inhale and falls as you exhale, a pattern the vagus nerve helps regulate. Those beat-to-beat differences contribute to heart rate variability, or HRV.
A 2022 meta-analysis published in Psychiatry and Clinical Neurosciences found that people with anxiety disorders tended to have lower parasympathetic activity at rest. In other words, the part of the nervous system that helps you wind down may be less active in people with anxiety. But that doesn’t necessarily mean the vagus nerve itself isn’t working properly.
For the most part, it does. Your vagus nerve isn’t a muscle that becomes weak because you forgot to exercise it, and it generally doesn’t need to be “reset.”
The problem, Gevirtz says, can be spending long stretches of time in that withdrawn state when life—and let’s be honest, the world—feels like a lot. He compares the nervous system to a thermostat: What matters isn’t making it stronger, but how readily it can shift when circumstances change.
The things you can do at home don’t directly stimulate the vagus nerve in the same way medical treatments do. (More on that below.) Dr. Austelle, who researches vagus nerve stimulation, says these techniques are better understood as behaviors that “influence” vagus nerve function.
That influence can happen in a few different ways. Here are five techniques to try.
“One of the techniques with the most evidence and the most convincing evidence is slow breathing,” Dr. Austelle says. A 2022 systematic review and meta-analysis published in Neuroscience & Biobehavioral Reviews looked at more than 200 studies and found that slow breathing increased signs of parasympathetic activity—the “rest, digest and restore” side of the nervous system—both while people were breathing slowly and afterward. The effect was also seen in studies where people practiced slow breathing over time.
Gevirtz generally recommends slowing to about four to seven breaths per minute. That works out to one full inhale-and-exhale cycle roughly every nine to 15 seconds—not holding your breath, just breathing more slowly and continuously. “It has to be effortless breathing,” he says.
Dr. Austelle says the exhale may be particularly important. To try it, sit comfortably, gradually slow your breathing and let your exhale last a little longer than your inhale. Don’t force enormous breaths; if you feel lightheaded, return to your normal breathing.
Cyclic sighing gives you a more specific pattern to follow. Inhale slowly through your nose, take a second, smaller inhale to fill your lungs a little more, and then slowly and fully exhale through your mouth. There isn’t a specific number of seconds you need to hit; the emphasis is on that double inhale followed by a longer exhale.
A 2023 study published in Cell Reports Medicine had adults practice cyclic sighing, two other breathing exercises or mindfulness meditation for five minutes a day over about a month. All four groups reported less anxiety, but the breathing exercises led to bigger improvements in positive mood, with cyclic sighing also producing the largest drop in respiratory rate.
Humming has a plausible connection to vagal activity, but the research here is considerably thinner. Gevirtz says some yoga practices pair humming with slow breathing, and the extended exhale may be doing much of the work. While it’s possible that humming adds something on its own, especially due to the proximity of the vocal cords to the vagus nerve, there isn’t enough evidence to say for sure.
A 2023 study published in Cureus measured HRV in 23 people during Bhramari, a yoga breathing technique that involves a humming exhale. Researchers found HRV changes consistent with lower physiological stress, but a study that small can’t tell us whether humming reliably reduces anxiety or offers benefits beyond slow breathing.
If you find it soothing, though, humming through a slow exhale is easy enough to try.
Cold exposure can trigger vagal activity, but its effects are more complicated than “cold equals calm.” Dr. Austelle points to the diving reflex, a response that kicks in when your face is exposed to cold and eventually helps slow your heart rate. A 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis published in Psychophysiology found increased cardiac vagal activity during facial cooling and water immersion, although the included studies were small and the quality of evidence was limited.
There’s a catch, though: Dr. Austelle says very cold temperatures initially activate the sympathetic nervous system, so your heart rate and blood pressure can actually rise before the diving reflex begins to have its slowing effect. In other words, an ice bath isn’t simply flipping on “rest and digest.” If cool water feels calming, briefly splashing or cooling your face is a less dramatic place to start.
You may also see advice to put something cold over the center of your chest. There’s much less research on that approach. In a small 2025 study, applying a cold pack to the chest for 20 minutes lowered participants’ heart rates and changed some measures of HRV, but it also raised blood pressure, and the study didn’t establish that stimulating the vagus nerve was responsible. For now, the connection between facial cooling and the diving reflex is much better established.
HRV biofeedback is essentially slow breathing with real-time feedback about how your heart is responding. A sensor tracks your heartbeat as you breathe, which can help you find the breathing pace that produces the strongest HRV response for you instead of simply following a one-size-fits-all pace. And it isn’t limited to a clinician’s office. Consumer sensors and phone-based tools can be used for HRV biofeedback at home, though Gevirtz cautions against treating the numbers from a smartwatch or other wearable as gospel. These devices tend to be better at measuring heart rate than HRV, he says, and day-to-day scores can be noisy enough that they’re not worth fixating on.
Gevirtz helped develop the HRV biofeedback approach with Paul Lehrer, PhD, a professor of psychiatry at Rutgers University who studies biofeedback and psychophysiology. With practice, Gevirtz says, that feedback can help people learn what the pattern feels like well enough to reproduce it without watching the numbers every time.
There’s also some evidence those changes can last. In a 2024 randomized controlled study published in Applied Psychophysiology and Biofeedback, people who completed HRV-biofeedback training showed greater improvements in resting HRV than an active control group. They weren’t significantly less anxious overall, suggesting that the improvement in HRV didn’t necessarily translate to less anxiety, but it did show that the intervention changed how their bodies were responding.
“It definitely has an effect for most people very quickly,” Gevirtz says. In his clinical work, patients who have practiced slow breathing can produce noticeable changes in their heart-rate pattern after only a few breaths. At the four-to-seven-breaths-per-minute pace he generally recommends, that means those physiological changes can begin within about a minute, although how quickly you actually feel calmer can vary.
A small 2026 pilot study suggests even one minute may be enough to make a difference in how anxious you feel. Researchers had 47 university students use either cyclic sighing, box breathing or no breathing exercise during real-life moments of acute stress. Five minutes later, both breathing groups reported larger drops in anxiety than the control group.
Regular practice may make it easier to get that calming effect over time, particularly with slow breathing. In his clinical work, Gevirtz has patients practice for about 10 minutes a day so the technique becomes more familiar before they need it during a stressful moment.
The 2023 Cell Reports Medicine study offers another clue: Participants practiced cyclic sighing for five minutes a day for about a month, and researchers measured their mood before and after each daily session. The more consistently people practiced, the bigger the mood boost after each session tended to be.
So when you see advice about how to stimulate the vagus nerve, it may be more useful to think about practicing ways to help your nervous system shift back toward calm rather than “toning” one specific nerve.
Actual VNS is different: These devices stimulate the nerve directly with electricity. According to the National Institute of Mental Health, implanted VNS is used for certain medical conditions, including treatment-resistant epilepsy and depression. Noninvasive, or transcutaneous, VNS delivers electrical stimulation through the skin and is being studied for a range of psychiatric and neurological conditions.
For everyday stress management, though, Gevirtz says evidence for commercial noninvasive devices remains mixed, particularly when researchers compare them with sham devices that feel similar but don’t provide the same stimulation.
For now, slowing your breathing is a much cheaper place to start.
These techniques can be useful when anxiety is making your whole system feel revved up, but they can’t address every reason you might be anxious. If you’re anxious most of the time, having panic attacks, losing sleep over it or starting to avoid parts of your life because of it, that’s worth bringing to a health-care or mental-health professional.
And sometimes the problem really is the problem. Breathing more slowly may help you feel steadier before a difficult conversation, but it won’t make the conversation disappear. It can, however, make it easier to walk into that conversation without feeling like your body has decided it’s an emergency.
That’s really the point for me. I’m not trying to breathe my way out of having problems. But it’s powerful to know I can use something as simple as my breathing to actually turn down the volume on anxiety when it starts taking over.

At Reader’s Digest, we’re committed to producing high-quality content by writers with expertise and experience in their field in consultation with relevant, qualified experts. We rely on reputable primary sources, including government and professional organizations and academic institutions as well as our writers’ personal experiences where appropriate. For this piece on how to stimulate the vagus nerve, Miranda Manier tapped her longtime experience as a journalist and health editor to ensure that all information is accurate and offers the best possible advice to readers. A sensor tracks your heartbeat as you breathe, which can help you find the breathing pace that produces the strongest HRV response for you instead of simply following a one-size-fits-all pace. And it isn’t limited to a clinician’s office. Consumer sensors and phone-based tools can be used for HRV biofeedback at home, though Gevirtz cautions against treating the numbers from a smartwatch or other wearable as gospel. These devices tend to be better at measuring heart rate than HRV, he says, and day-to-day scores can be noisy enough that they’re not worth fixating on.

Gevirtz helped develop the HRV biofeedback approach with Paul Lehrer, PhD, a professor of psychiatry at Rutgers University who studies biofeedback and psychophysiology. With practice, Gevirtz says, that feedback can help people learn what the pattern feels like well enough to reproduce it without watching the numbers every time.

There’s also some evidence those changes can last. In a 2024 randomized controlled study published in Applied Psychophysiology and Biofeedback, people who completed HRV-biofeedback training showed greater improvements in resting HRV than an active control group. They weren’t significantly less anxious overall, suggesting that the improvement in HRV didn’t necessarily translate to less anxiety, but it did show that the intervention changed how their bodies were responding.

How quickly can these techniques calm you down?

“It definitely has an effect for most people very quickly,” Gevirtz says. In his clinical work, patients who have practiced slow breathing can produce noticeable changes in their heart-rate pattern after only a few breaths. At the four-to-seven-breaths-per-minute pace he generally recommends, that means those physiological changes can begin within about a minute, although how quickly you actually feel calmer can vary.

A small 2026 pilot study suggests even one minute may be enough to make a difference in how anxious you feel. Researchers had 47 university students use either cyclic sighing, box breathing or no breathing exercise during real-life moments of acute stress. Five minutes later, both breathing groups reported larger drops in anxiety than the control group.

Will stimulating your vagus nerve reduce your anxiety and stress levels overall?

Regular practice may make it easier to get that calming effect over time, particularly with slow breathing. In his clinical work, Gevirtz has patients practice for about 10 minutes a day so the technique becomes more familiar before they need it during a stressful moment.

The 2023 Cell Reports Medicine study offers another clue: Participants practiced cyclic sighing for five minutes a day for about a month, and researchers measured their mood before and after each daily session. The more consistently people practiced, the bigger the mood boost after each session tended to be.

So when you see advice about how to stimulate the vagus nerve, it may be more useful to think about practicing ways to help your nervous system shift back toward calm rather than “toning” one specific nerve.

What about vagus nerve stimulators?

Actual VNS is different: These devices stimulate the nerve directly with electricity. According to the National Institute of Mental Health, implanted VNS is used for certain medical conditions, including treatment-resistant epilepsy and depression. Noninvasive, or transcutaneous, VNS delivers electrical stimulation through the skin and is being studied for a range of psychiatric and neurological conditions.

For everyday stress management, though, Gevirtz says evidence for commercial noninvasive devices remains mixed, particularly when researchers compare them with sham devices that feel similar but don’t provide the same stimulation.

For now, slowing your breathing is a much cheaper place to start.

When is anxiety bigger than a breathing exercise?

These techniques can be useful when anxiety is making your whole system feel revved up, but they can’t address every reason you might be anxious. If you’re anxious most of the time, having panic attacks, losing sleep over it or starting to avoid parts of your life because of it, that’s worth bringing to a health-care or mental-health professional.

And sometimes the problem really is the problem. Breathing more slowly may help you feel steadier before a difficult conversation, but it won’t make the conversation disappear. It can, however, make it easier to walk into that conversation without feeling like your body has decided it’s an emergency.

That’s really the point for me. I’m not trying to breathe my way out of having problems. But it’s powerful to know I can use something as simple as my breathing to actually turn down the volume on anxiety when it starts taking over.

articles.title: Here’s How “Six Degrees of Kevin Bacon” Originated—And Why You Might Actually Be Six Degrees Away from Him Too
articles.content:
We’ve all had those it’s-a-small-world moments when we discover we’re randomly connected to someone else. It happened to me recently while traveling in Athens, Greece, where I struck up a new friendship with a fellow traveler from Italy. We quickly discovered, to our surprise, that we had a mutual friend.
You’ve most likely heard of the theory six degrees of separation, which suggests that everyone on Earth is connected through a chain of no more than six people. Theoretically, that means you could trace your connection to just about anyone, whether it’s a person you just met in a foreign country, like I did, or a famous Hollywood star.
Of course, this concept is best illustrated with one particular Hollywood star, in the popular parlor game Six Degrees of Kevin Bacon, where players attempt to connect any actor to Kevin Bacon through the films on their résumé. For example, Christian Slater is just one degree away, having starred alongside Bacon in 1995’s Murder in the First. The late James Dean, meanwhile, is an iconic actor from generations ago, but he’s still just three degrees away—Dean appeared with Dennis Hopper in 1955’s Rebel Without a Cause, Hopper starred with Chris Penn in the 1993 movie True Romance, and Penn and Bacon were both in the ’80s classic Footloose.
Six Degrees of Kevin Bacon demonstrates how surprisingly short the paths between people can be. Still, there are some questions to consider. As a former celebrity journalist, for example, I once interviewed Bacon at a party. Does that count as a connection to him since it was so fleeting? And does the theory translate to everyday people around the globe, both with and without Kevin Bacon in the mix?
To get to the bottom of this, I spoke with Albert-László Barabási, PhD, who teaches at Northeastern University and Harvard Medical School and researches complex networks, and Jure Leskovec, PhD, a computer science professor at Stanford University. Read on to learn how the game got its start, plus whether the underlying concept behind Six Degrees of Kevin Bacon actually holds up to scientific scrutiny—and what it could mean for you.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more fun facts, humor, cleaning, travel and tech all week long.
Three friends—Brian Turtle, Mike Ginelli and Craig Fass—came up with the concept as a college drinking game when they were students at Albright College in Pennsylvania more than 30 years ago. “We were just a couple of college guys who watched movies like JFK and Footloose, and found that in 1994, Kevin Bacon was everywhere,” Turtle said on the People of Play online gaming community of the pastime that “took on a life of its own.”
The Six Degrees of Kevin Bacon game, he joked, “was kind of a ‘stupid human trick,’” but it was one that got the college pals interviewed by everyone from Jon Stewart to Howard Stern. In 1996, the trio even created a board game, produced by the newly formed company Endless Games, where Turtle has worked ever since. “After graduation in ’95, I never thought I’d hear about [Six Degrees of Kevin Bacon] again, but it never went away!” he said.
Six Degrees of Kevin Bacon became popular in the 1990s, but the idea behind it is based on real research and theories that go back much further. In the 1960s, Yale psychologist Stanley Milgram conducted a “small world” experiment to explore how closely people were linked via their social networks. He asked participants to attempt to get letters to a specific person by forwarding them to acquaintances they believed might help get the letters closer to their destination. (More on how that experiment went in a minute.)
The idea that actors can be linked to Kevin Bacon—or that two seemingly random people can be connected—through a short chain of acquaintances does indeed hold up. And those ties may be much smaller than six degrees, according to research. Here’s how it shakes out.
You’d be hard-pressed not to find a connection between Bacon and nearly any other working actor. Because actors often appear in multiple films with different co-stars, their projects create a sprawling web of work that can be used to trace a path to Bacon.
Don’t believe it? The website Oracle of Bacon lets you enter an actor’s name and see how they’re connected to him, step by step. Even some pretty obscure actors in the database can be linked to Bacon through his network. Ever heard of the Croatian actor Rade Šerbedźija? Maybe not, but he’s just one degree from Bacon, thanks to the film X-Men: First Class.
The broader six degrees of separation theory can be applied to link anyone to Bacon. Yes, anyone—including you! Barabási, who’s a pioneer in network science, says we may be connected to almost anyone in the world not by six degrees, but by as few as three to four steps, even if only through a chain of acquaintances.
“A typical person knows about 1,000 people on a first-name basis, so there are roughly—and this is a simplification, but it works—1,000 × 1,000 people two handshakes away and 10^9 people (10 to the ninth power, or 1 followed by nine zeros) three handshakes away,” he says. For those who aren’t so mathematically inclined, that’s 1 million people two steps away, and 1 billion people three steps away, and each additional step expands that network exponentially. “That is the secret of six degrees.”
But throw in social media, and the definition of a connection makes the picture a little more complicated. According to Nature Reviews Physics, Milgram’s letter chains typically ranged from two to 10 links, but today’s technology and online social networks have reduced those connection numbers massively. Just think of all the people you’re technically “friends” with on Facebook or connected to on LinkedIn—and how many of those same people you wouldn’t recognize by name.
Leskovec, whose research spans network science, AI and machine learning, examined Microsoft’s instant-messaging network and found two people were separated by an average of 6.6 steps in the network of approximately 240 million people. “It does not mean everyone was directly connected,” he explains. “Rather, local circles overlap enough that only a handful of steps usually link people across the network.”
In 2016, Facebook revealed that the average separation between two users on its platform had shrunk to 3.57 degrees, down from 3.74 in 2011. That’s an incredibly small number on a network that spans billions of people, and it’s likely getting smaller. Still, a short chain of online connections doesn’t equate to really knowing someone.
So six degrees of separation isn’t a hard-and-fast rule, but the separation between people is shockingly small. “‘Six degrees’ is best understood as a memorable approximation of typical connectivity, not a universal upper bound,” Leskovec says.
Turtle, the man who co-created Six Degrees of Kevin Bacon, says that the actor wasn’t thrilled with the game at first because “he thought we were making fun of him.”
That began to change in 1995, when Turtle and his friends were on The Jon Stewart Show to demonstrate their uncanny knack for tracing any Hollywood actor back to Bacon, who was also a guest on the program that night. “Somebody with a bigger ego might have told us to go pound sand, but Kevin warmed up to the game and even wound up writing a rather hilarious prologue to that bestselling paperback [on the topic],” Turtle wrote on People of Play.
Once Bacon realized the game was all in good fun, he embraced it and took the idea a step further by founding SixDegrees.org—a nonprofit foundation that uses storytelling and community-first campaigns to bring people together and fight disconnection in society.
Well, you probably shouldn’t call up Kevin Bacon and tell him you know him through a friend. But by all means, continue playing the game! It’s neat to think about the larger idea of discovering connections between people, whether it’s linking actors to Kevin Bacon or finding ties within our own social circles.
The concept also offers a great reminder that we’re all more connected than it may first appear. Through family relationships, friendships and even chance encounters, our seemingly separate worlds often overlap in surprising ways. As Bacon notes in a video for SixDegrees.org, it’s all about “thinking about the connections that we all have.”
And it’s important to keep in mind that those connections affect society, for better or worse. As Leskovec notes, “it matters because information, opportunities, behaviors (and sometimes misinformation or disease) can spread across a large population very quickly.” In other words, the world is small and our influence is outsized, so go forth and do good.

articles.content:
On a Wednesday evening, a group of women is gathered at Mimi’s Needlepoint in Dallas, their hands moving thread through canvas, their conversations easy and unhurried. Someone’s working on a Christmas ornament. Someone else is stitching a bag charm. A few of them have become so close that they coordinate which weekly Sip & Stitch sessions to attend together and make plans to hang out outside of the store.
Madeline Alford, 35, co-owner of Mimi’s Needlepoint, is amazed by it all. A few years ago, she left her career in New York City and moved back to Dallas after spending more than 10 years in what she describes as “the corporate grind of working 8 to 6, coming home, doomscrolling, watching the news and going to bed, and then doing it all over again,” before she and her cousin Amelia Alford, 30, decided to do something different. They started an online canvas design company that has grown into a brick-and-mortar store—and now a community. “It’s a third place,” Alford says, “somewhere people can come and hang out, make friends and learn this very analog craft.” (The sociologist Ray Oldenburg coined the term third place in 1989 to describe somewhere that isn’t home or work.)
According to Alford, the biggest challenge since opening their doors has been the supply chain, which tells you something about this growing movement. Needlepoint has exploded so fast, she explains, that there’s a shortage of the canvas itself. Thread is hard to come by too. “You’ll go to needlepoint stores, and none of us are fully stocked,” she says.
Something is happening across America, and not just with needlepoint.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more true stories, life hacks, fun facts, humor, cleaning, travel and tech all week long.
Over the past few years, younger generations have taken up so-called “old-school” hobbies with gusto. Gen Zers are joining knitting and mahjong clubs in numbers that are surprising even to the people who run these groups. And Millennials are buying landlines for their kids to delay giving them smartphones. Independent bookstores and specialty magazine stores are popping up in cities across the country. Pen pals are coming back into fashion. Bird-watching has taken flight. Bread baking is on the rise. The common thread here is tactile activities, which more people are seeking out as they shy away from screen time.
Those who study leisure and well-being aren’t surprised. Research published in the journal Nature Medicine in 2023 found that people who reported having at least one hobby showed fewer symptoms of depression and higher levels of happiness, health and life satisfaction. A separate study published in the Journal of Global Health in 2025 found that adults who engaged in regular hobbies had a 29% lower risk of mortality. But the benefits, researchers note, aren’t limited to a single age group or hobby.
Robert Waldinger, MD, is a psychiatrist and the director of the Harvard Study of Adult Development, which is one of the longest-running studies of human happiness ever conducted. Dr. Waldinger has spent decades trying to understand what makes people thrive, and his research keeps pointing to the same answer: other people.
“When we asked people in their 80s what they were proudest of,” he says, “it was always about people. It was always, ‘I was a good spouse. I was a good parent. I was a good mentor.’ It was never about winning a prize or making money.” But personal connection feels more elusive than ever. Part of the problem, says Dr. Waldinger, is what the digital world does to our perception of reality.
“Never before,” he explains, “have we been as confused and uncertain about what’s real. Is this person online real, or is it a bot? What am I seeing in the news? What am I not seeing?” That constant uncertainty, he explains, is corrosive to our well-being. But in person, the doubt dissolves. “I see with my eyes,” he says. “It’s tangible. I believe it. I see who this person is.”
Lindsay Degen, 38, first tried knitting as a child. Her grandmother taught her how to cast on and cast off, but they didn’t live close to each other, so the lessons happened sporadically, during visits. Over the years, Degen developed an interest in fashion and went on to study textiles at Rhode Island School of Design, then launched a knitting club over Zoom during COVID-19 because she felt isolated at home.
That group was small at first, but it quickly grew into an online community that she named Knit Club. In 2024, she opened a brick-and-mortar store with the same name in Providence, Rhode Island. Its calendar is packed with knitting circles, beginner boot camps and a roster of events that pair knitting with just about anything: Lord of the Rings marathons. Drag nights. Purl and Swirl gatherings with wine from the shop down the street.
The store hosts free Craft Circles twice a week. “The one on Tuesday is rowdy,” Degen says, smiling, “while the one on Sunday is chill and sweet.” Both draw college students, 70-somethings and everyone in between. The motto is “All Crafters Welcome!” You don’t even have to knit: “You can show up and draw,” says Degen. “You can do anything you want, as long as it’s not wet.”
Degen admits knitting blurs the line between her work and her leisure, but that’s part of the attraction: “I’ve made my job out of my hobby, so I go home from work and I knit … but then am I actually still at my job?”
She suspects a lot of people share that restlessness. What knitting offers, she says, is visible, measurable progress as you see something building, row by row. “A lot of people say knitting is Zen,” she says. “I don’t think that’s necessarily true when you’re a beginner. It can be really challenging. But overcoming the challenge and seeing your thing build is super rewarding.”

articles.content:
Someone in my life who shall rename nameless (you know exactly who you are) is a scream sneezer. It is the loudest sneeze you’ve ever heard, and he manages to make it sound like he’s screaming AH SH*T—although he swears he’s not cursing on purpose. It’s so loud that it has woken our deaf dog out of a deep sleep, made more than one baby cry and set off a car alarm. I am not kidding. At this point, I’m less concerned about his sinuses than I am about whether our homeowners insurance covers sonic weapons.
Thus far, I have not punched him, but every sneeze startles me so badly that I fear the day is coming. I don’t want to be the first person convicted of assaulting someone for having a functioning respiratory system, but I also can’t comfortably rule it out.
If you’ve never been around a scream sneezer, I envy your innocence. They are a small but disproportionately terrifying percentage of the population, and once you’ve encountered one, your nervous system is permanently changed. You will forever brace yourself whenever someone in the vicinity inhales a little too deeply because a perfectly ordinary sneeze becomes a potential jump scare.
So, yes, scream sneezing is certainly alarming. And frustrating. And annoying. And an affront to “use your indoor voice.” But is it actually rude? After all, my loved one—yes, I still love him—swears that he isn’t trying to be so loud. He claims that his sneezes simply emerge dramatically, like a firework going off in a library. He swears he is not deliberately trying to frighten small children or make the dog question its place in the universe. I am not so sure.
Let’s chat about this.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more etiquette, humor, cleaning, travel, tech and fun facts all week long.
I am not the only person bothered by scream sneezes, and generally speaking, anything that makes a significant portion of the population want to throw a shoe at you deserves at least an etiquette investigation. So why does it feel so rude? Two factors: loudness and germs.
Scream sneezes aren’t just loud; they are loud loud. A study conducted by Noise Measurement Systems found that the average male sneeze is around 90 decibels when measured from 2 feet away. That’s roughly as loud as a blender running at full speed, except the blender has the decency to have a lid. The noise level does depend on the sneezer’s physiology—smaller lungs make quieter sneezes, for instance—so if the average is at 90 decibels, then scream sneezers could be entering jet-engine territory. So while I couldn’t find exact numbers for the volume of my loved one’s scream sneezes, I can report that he has made me question whether our windows are double-paned.
A sneeze is not merely a noise. It is a biological event involving a rapidly expelled mixture of droplets and particles and … other, potentially infectious, things. MIT researchers studying sneeze dynamics found that larger droplets can travel several feet, while smaller particles may travel up to 20 feet, depending on conditions. The exact distance depends on the sneeze and the surrounding environment, and we don’t know that a louder sneeze necessarily sends germs farther. Still, if someone is going to unleash a respiratory weather event in your direction, you would prefer they at least attempt to contain it.
A scream sneeze, then, combines two of the most universally disliked things in public life: an unnecessarily loud noise and the possibility of being involuntarily included in someone else’s germ-distribution system.
My loved one claims that because sneezing is a natural bodily function, it is exempt from etiquette. This is an interesting legal defense. I look forward to hearing him explain it to the next person who crop-dusts an elevator. Natural bodily functions are not, in fact, exempt from etiquette. We have rules about all sorts of them.
Etiquette does not require us to pretend our bodies don’t do strange things. It asks us to manage those things with reasonable consideration for everyone else.
Of course, not all bodily functions are equally controllable. Sneezing is a reflex, and trying to forcibly suppress a sneeze can actually be harmful, potentially damaging your eardrums and even rupturing blood vessels in extreme cases, according to the Cleveland Clinic. We should not expect anyone to achieve perfect control over something their body does without permission. But the question isn’t whether or not sneezing is rude—as long as you cover your mouth, you’re fine—but the screaming aspect of it.
I couldn’t find any research about how much control people have over the volume of their sneezes. Researchers have apparently been too busy studying important things like the trajectory of airborne pathogens to settle the disputes that actually matter to society. And I’m willing to entertain the possibility that some people genuinely cannot reduce the volume much. We all have different bodies, reflexes and medical circumstances.
But I also suspect that some scream sneezers have simply never considered whether they could do anything differently. When you’ve spent your entire life sneezing like a car backfiring, it may not occur to you that other people find it startling.
So, no, you cannot reasonably be expected to control what you genuinely cannot control. But you also can be reasonably expected to care about the effect you have on other people—especially when that effect may result in a mini cardiac event or a shower of germs.
My loved one scream sneezes straight into whatever or whoever is in front of him. He says the sneeze comes on so quickly that he can’t do anything about it. He also dislikes covering his mouth because then he gets snot on his hands. This is the part of his argument I find particularly compelling, in the sense that I find it compelling evidence that he has misunderstood the entire purpose of etiquette. He would rather distribute his mucus among innocent bystanders than briefly inconvenience himself.
A big part of scream sneezing is where it is happening and who is affected. For instance, if you’re at home by yourself, do whatever you like. But once others are around, especially if it’s in a crowded, public venue, that changes the noise calculus. It also matters who is around you. A scream sneeze is more consequential around sleeping babies, startled animals, people with sensory sensitivities or anyone who may be particularly vulnerable to respiratory infections.
Similar to the etiquette around telling someone you’re sick, the etiquette requirements here are not especially demanding.
I don’t know about you, but my first reaction when I’m startled is fear, anger and the desire to investigate whether I’m legally permitted to throw something. But punching the sneezer would definitely be rude—far ruder than the scream sneeze itself. It is also rude to shame someone, mock their medical circumstances or insist that they must be doing it on purpose. Even if you (and I) suspect that a person could control the volume at least somewhat, we cannot know what is happening inside their body. Offer grace … and perhaps a tissue.
If the behavior is genuinely affecting you, especially if the person repeatedly sneezes uncovered in your direction, it is reasonable to ask them to cover their mouth or turn away.
Scream sneezing is not inherently rude, but refusing to do anything to mitigate it is. While sneezing is a reflex, involuntary does not equal consequence-free. My ruling? The sneeze itself is innocent; the mucus distribution strategy is where things get legally interesting. My loved one, for instance, may be acquitted of the noise charge due to insufficient evidence of intent. But the charge of sneezing directly onto other people because he doesn’t want to get snot on his own hands? That case is going to trial.
And I would like the record to show that the dog is available as a witness.

And I’m willing to entertain the possibility that some people genuinely cannot reduce the volume much. We all have different bodies, reflexes and medical circumstances.

But I also suspect that some scream sneezers have simply never considered whether they could do anything differently. When you’ve spent your entire life sneezing like a car backfiring, it may not occur to you that other people find it startling.

So, no, you cannot reasonably be expected to control what you genuinely cannot control. But you also can be reasonably expected to care about the effect you have on other people—especially when that effect may result in a mini cardiac event or a shower of germs.

How to scream sneeze without being rude

My loved one scream sneezes straight into whatever or whoever is in front of him. He says the sneeze comes on so quickly that he can’t do anything about it. He also dislikes covering his mouth because then he gets snot on his hands. This is the part of his argument I find particularly compelling, in the sense that I find it compelling evidence that he has misunderstood the entire purpose of etiquette. He would rather distribute his mucus among innocent bystanders than briefly inconvenience himself.

A big part of scream sneezing is where it is happening and who is affected. For instance, if you’re at home by yourself, do whatever you like. But once others are around, especially if it’s in a crowded, public venue, that changes the noise calculus. It also matters who is around you. A scream sneeze is more consequential around sleeping babies, startled animals, people with sensory sensitivities or anyone who may be particularly vulnerable to respiratory infections.

Similar to the etiquette around telling someone you’re sick, the etiquette requirements here are not especially demanding.

  • Warn. Some sneezes surprise everyone, including the sneezer themselves. But often you do have a bit of warning that one is coming. Use this time to warn people around you (“Sneeze incoming!”) and turn or move away to minimize the blast zone.
  • Cover. You should always cover your sneeze. If you have time to grab a tissue, great. Otherwise, sneezing into your sleeve, the collar of your T-shirt or even your hands is better than just letting it fly through the air. Yes, you may get snot on yourself. This is a regrettable but manageable consequence of having a nose. (And please sanitize your hands afterward.)
  • Muffle. At least try to do something to reduce the noise level of the sneeze, whether that’s quickly walking into another room or using something to muffle your scream, like a towel or thick coat to sneeze into. That said, nobody needs to contort themselves into a pretzel trying to silence a reflex. The goal is reasonable consideration, not sneeze perfection.
  • Prevent. My loved one sneezes a lot due to allergies yet can’t remember to take the medication that would reduce all of his allergy symptoms, scream sneezing included. If allergies regularly turn you into a human confetti cannon, consider managing them with appropriate measures or discussing treatment options with a health-care professional. You don’t need to medicate yourself solely to make other people happy, but reducing symptoms may improve your own comfort as well as the comfort of those around you.
  • Apologize. If you do happen to scream sneeze and startle and/or spray everyone, just offer a quick “I’m so sorry!” An apology is not an admission of guilt. It is simply a way of saying “I recognize that you were just minding your business when my face suddenly became a percussion instrument.”
  • Clean. Just because you do it in public does not make it a community art installation. If you’ve sprayed mucus onto a table, counter or other shared surface, wipe it up appropriately and wash your hands.

What to do if you’re on the receiving end of a scream sneeze

I don’t know about you, but my first reaction when I’m startled is fear, anger and the desire to investigate whether I’m legally permitted to throw something. But punching the sneezer would definitely be rude—far ruder than the scream sneeze itself. It is also rude to shame someone, mock their medical circumstances or insist that they must be doing it on purpose. Even if you (and I) suspect that a person could control the volume at least somewhat, we cannot know what is happening inside their body. Offer grace … and perhaps a tissue.

If the behavior is genuinely affecting you, especially if the person repeatedly sneezes uncovered in your direction, it is reasonable to ask them to cover their mouth or turn away.

The verdict

Scream sneezing is not inherently rude, but refusing to do anything to mitigate it is. While sneezing is a reflex, involuntary does not equal consequence-free. My ruling? The sneeze itself is innocent; the mucus distribution strategy is where things get legally interesting. My loved one, for instance, may be acquitted of the noise charge due to insufficient evidence of intent. But the charge of sneezing directly onto other people because he doesn’t want to get snot on his own hands? That case is going to trial.

And I would like the record to show that the dog is available as a witness.
